text:
Europe's diesel summer vs winter specifications

The main difference is on CFPP which is Cold Filter Plugging Point. 

CFPP is the lowest temperature at which diesel can still pass through a standardized filter under specified test conditions. Below this temperature, wax crystals can form and block the fuel filter, potentially stopping fuel flow to the engine.

To bring down CFPP, you can blend in more jet fuel and/or use an additive called a cold flow improver.

The transition starts in October. So we are going to get some help from jet soon.

By "little pressure", we meant "logistical pressure", not economic. Some of you folks just don't get it.

No, this is false.

1) This is just a preliminary daily flow print from Kpler. Kpler explicitly flags these as raw estimates, and these prints carry a heavy upward revision bias weeks down the road.

2) Since everyone is now issuing spot tenders following ADNOC's playbook, we can roughly deduce the volumes they are able to transit.

China just took down sizable clips of Basrah and Arab crude via tender—loading outside the Strait. Both SOMO and Aramco are running ADNOC’s exact playbook. Shuttling crude into Fujairah for offshore STS.

3) TD3C freight is ripping. That’s not floating storage parking barrels; it’s genuine tanker demand driven by barrels actively clearing through STS ops.

4) Optical and SAR satellite feeds confirm nonstop liftings out of UAE terminals like Zirku and Das. Iraq and Kuwait are lifting at a steady clip too, even if trailing ADNOC's pace.

5) So while Bessent quoting 16mb/d was blatant jawboning—maybe cherry picking a single day spike as the baseline—don't let permabull bias blind you into discounting shadow flows.

More in my regular Monday COT update.

COT update on #forex covering the week to 18 August. Ahead of the dollar tumble following last Wednesday’s US Treasury bond buyback announcement, speculators made a third consecutive, albeit modest, weekly reduction in bullish dollar bets.
Overall, the non-commercial USD long against eight IMM futures was reduced by USD 1.3 billion to USD 35.7 billion, with notable buying of CAD and CHF partly offset by selling of JPY and AUD.
Worth noting that when the Dollar Index and the broader Bloomberg Dollar Index last traded near current levels three months ago, the combined dollar long was just USD 5 billion. The subsequent build-up in bullish exposure highlights the number of positions potentially caught offside by last week’s sharp dollar reversal.

Commodities Weekly: Weather, war and debt broaden the commodity rally
Broad-based commodity gains gather momentum as weather risks, geopolitical disruption, tight supply and US fiscal concerns drive strength across energy, metals and agriculture. https://t.co/bV3M9ueSpl via @saxobank

Copper stocks monitored by the three major futures exchanges rose by 59 kt this week, the first increase in ten weeks, lifting combined inventories back above 1 million tonnes. Inflows were recorded across all three exchanges, led by the LME with a 33.6 kt increase, followed by SHFE at 19.8 kt, while COMEX stocks rose by another 5.7 kt, marking a 19th consecutive weekly increase.

The bulk of global exchange-monitored copper inventories remains concentrated in COMEX warehouses, which now account for 67% of the total, down from 71% last week. After nine consecutive weeks of falling combined inventories, the latest increase offers some tentative relief to an otherwise tight visible supply picture, although the continued concentration of metal in the US remains a key feature of the market.

#Gold continues its strong run higher, gaining 1.8% on the day and 5.1% on the week to trade at USD 4,600, well above the 200-day MA which was the technical trigger for fresh momentum buying and now also above the 0.382 Fibonacci retracement of the January to June correction at USD 4,574. Next level being the 0.5 retracement and May local high around USD 4,770.
Silver trades up 8.1% on the week, while platinum has added 8.8%

#Commodities
Weather, war, fiscal debt concerns, and a softer dollar all supporting broad-based commodity gains this week, with the BCOM TR index rising around 3%, lifting its YTD return to 30%. All sectors except industrial metals traded higher, led by soft commodities with gains of around 5%, followed by precious metals and energy, also near 5%, while grains trailed with a roughly 3% advance. At the individual commodity level, platinum, silver, crude oil, diesel, sugar and cocoa all recorded gains of more than 5%, highlighting the increasingly broad nature of the current rally.
#CrudeOil: Brent rose to its highest level in almost four weeks near USD 95 after President Trump threatened Iran with economic warfare, before paring the advance to trade near USD 93.5, with WTI around USD 86.4. The US administration is expected to provide details on Monday about how it intends to further isolate Iran’s economy, with traders concerned that tougher measures could trigger significant blowback from China, a key trading partner and buyer of Iranian oil. With the Middle East crisis showing few signs of easing, the risk of further disruption to regional energy flows continues to support crude and refined product prices.
#Gold: Thursday’s setback, triggered partly by rising oil prices and renewed inflation concerns, proved temporary, with gold surging again as long-end Treasury yields climbed following a Bessent interview that failed to quell investor concerns about spiralling US debt and fiscal sustainability. The ability of gold to rally alongside higher nominal yields highlights the growing importance of fiscal and debt concerns as a driver of hard-asset demand. Gold is on track for a third consecutive weekly gain and could potentially secure a weekly close above its 200-day moving average, currently near USD 4,514, strengthening the technical recovery following its recent correction.
#Copper: The transition metal trades softer on the week as LME inventories head for their biggest weekly inflow since 2020, with traders delivering metal to profit from the recent supply squeeze. Despite the immediate relief, nearby spreads remain elevated and the market vulnerable after months of inventory outflows, much of it diverted to the US ahead of a potential tariff announcement. Underlying physical supply therefore remains tight, supporting the broader bullish outlook.
